title: Bounded-window KV cache with adaptive backpressure and graceful GPU-OOM fallback
creator: Leah Morgan
description:
Context: We're seeing tail-latency spikes and intermittent GPU OOMs in multi-tenant serving when long sequences lead to large KV residency. Current paged/blocked KV designs reduce average memory but cause sudden allocation pressure and head-of-line stalls when many long-context requests overlap.

Problem statement: We need a practical runtime-level strategy that: 1) bounds per-request KV working set growth using a windowed retention model, 2) signals and smooths load to upstream scheduling to avoid synchronous OOM cascades, and 3) provides a deterministic fallback path that preserves latency SLOs for short requests while allowing long requests to continue with degraded throughput.

Proposal summary: Implement a "bounded-window KV" mode that splits KV residency into fixed-duration windows (logical time slices of attention history) with the following features: 
- Soft retention limits per-request (N windows) with an LRU-like priority inside each window.
- Adaptive backpressure signals exposed to the scheduler: soft_shed and holdback tokens that throttle batching and admission for requests that would push resident set above a dynamic high-water mark.
- Graceful OOM fallback: when hard limit is reached, use a prioritized partial-eviction strategy (drop older windows for low-priority requests while preserving most-recent window + KV prefix cache for high-priority/latency-sensitive traffic).

Why different from existing approaches: Unlike slab-only or chunked allocators, windowed retention encodes temporal locality at a coarse granularity that simplifies eviction math and gives predictable worst-case resident set sizes. Combining this with explicit backpressure tokens reduces synchronous eviction storms that previously caused cascading tail latency.

Design links and artifacts: 
- Design doc (internal Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Bounded-Window-KV-Design
- Simulation notebooks (Drive): https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/1-window-sim
- Microbench harness (GitHub): https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra-kv-sim/pull/67

Implementation plan: 
1) Runtime data structure: implement per-request window table metadata (compact 16B entries per window pointer) and a global residency counter that tracks resident bytes per-window-weighted.
2) Admission controller: expose tokens from an admission service that inspects current residency vs. dynamic target and returns admit / delay / shed directives. Integrate with batching pipeline to delay low-priority requests before they enter KV allocations.
3) Eviction policy: prioritized window eviction with per-request priority and age heuristics. Implement fast path that can drop entire oldest windows without touching inner-page structures to keep CPU costs minimal.
4) Fallback path: for requests delayed or partially-evicted, route to a best-effort streaming execution that sacrifices throughput (smaller KV context, truncated attention) but keeps token latency within SLO for the top-k critical requests.

Performance targets: 
- Keep P95 token-level latency increase < 10% for latency-tier traffic under memory pressure test harness.
- Reduce frequency of GPU OOM events to < 1 per 10M tokens in stress tests.
- Maintain aggregate throughput > 75% of baseline for mixed workload in degraded mode.

Trade-offs and open questions: 
- Granularity of window: 64-token windows vs 256-token windows — larger windows give higher retention efficiency but coarser eviction control. Simulation suggests 128-token windows hit a good sweet spot for typical request distributions.
- Admission latency vs batching benefits: delaying requests to avoid OOM can reduce batch sizes and hurt throughput for some workloads. We plan conservative holdback thresholds tuned per-customer tier.
- Memory accounting complexity: per-window accounting gives predictable bounds but increases meta-data overhead; we aim for <0.6% memory overhead at 1M concurrent windows.

Acceptance criteria:
acceptance_criteria: Runtime exposes bounded-window mode toggled by config flag and defaults to off
Admission controller returns admit/delay/shed and integrates with existing batching pipeline
Eviction path can drop whole windows atomically without per-token ops
Benchmarks: P95 token latency delta < 10% for latency-tier traffic under stress
OOMs reduced to <1 per 10M tokens in stress harness
Documentation: Design doc, runbook, and operator dashboard tile for resident set and token holdback metrics

notes: 13-Feb: initial spike analysis — long tails caused by overlapping long-context interactive sessions from internal partner. Traces attached in Confluence.
02-Mar: simulation shows 128-token windows reduced peak resident set by ~38% for mixed workload; see sim notebook.
05-Mar: design review with SRE and Runtime teams — agreed on token-based admission and prioritized eviction. Follow-up: refine holdback thresholds per-customer tier.
09-Mar: prototype PR merged (partial): https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/2345 — includes window metadata and basic eviction. Next: admission controller integration.

12-Mar: stress run with prototype produced 3 OOMs over 50M tokens; failure analysis points to race when admission delayed batches are re-inserted. Plan: add epoch-based admission tokens to avoid double-allocation.
